books.section: Topic 6.10 Development of the Middle Class
The Rise of the Modern American City

primary_sources: Electric streetcars on Canal Street, New Orleans, Detroit Publishing Company postcard, 1907

stimulus.text: The image is a hand-colored postcard of Canal Street, New Orleans, copyrighted 1907 by the Detroit Publishing Company. It shows a wide city street with several sets of streetcar tracks running down its middle and three electric streetcars carrying passengers. Tall commercial buildings line both sides of the street, and a horse-drawn carriage stands at the right edge.
stimulus.source_note: Electric streetcars on Canal Street, New Orleans, 1907 postcard view (Detroit Publishing Company). Public domain image from Wikimedia Commons; viewed by the writer.

stem: Which chain of effects best explains how electric streetcars changed where the middle class lived?

options.text: Streetcars replaced railroads, so factories moved into city centers
options.misconception: Streetcars carried city passengers; they did not replace railroads or move factories.

options.text: Streetcars ended all walking, so families never left their neighborhoods
options.misconception: People kept walking; streetcars added a longer trip, they did not end walking.

options.text: Streetcars made travel from outlying areas practical, so families could live farther out
Streetcars carried freight across the country, so farmers shipped wheat by streetcar
options.misconception: Streetcars carried city passengers, not cross-country freight.

rationales.A: Railroads kept carrying freight and long-distance passengers. Streetcars served the city itself.
rationales.B: Walking continued. The change was that a family could live farther away and still get to work.
rationales.C: Cheap daily rides let families live beyond walking distance of downtown, buy homes there, and commute. Those outlying homes were the early suburbs.
rationales.D: Wheat traveled by railroad, not by streetcar. Streetcars moved people within the city.
rationales.general:
Follow the chain one link at a time.
1. Electric streetcars made fast, cheap rides across the city possible.
2. A worker could then live farther from the workplace and still arrive each day.
3. Background from the books: families moved to early suburbs, separating home from workplace.
4. Homeownership in those suburbs became the middle class's defining aspiration.
Remember: a chain answer must hold at every link, not only at the end.
